name: Karl Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a press brake at Kessler Metalcraft, where we make stainless steel counters and sinks for restaurant kitchens. A press brake is a big machine that folds sheet steel along a line, so I load the sheet, line it up against the back stops, fold, flip, fold again. I've been there eight months and my angles are still a degree out sometimes, which the welders love to point out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like turning a flat sheet into something real, a sink someone will wash pans in. I use AI apps all day, on my break I ask one to check my bend sums and at night I use one to design little 3D-printed parts I sell online. What wears me out is the pay, and the noise, and knowing my girlfriend Lena earns even less as a trainee hairdresser.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down but fine, the tools are still handy. At work I'd keep showing people the app that checks bend allowances, which is how much the steel stretches when you fold it. Online I'd post something like: still useful, just not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing changes for the job, and that's the problem, the pay's still low. Kessler is steady enough, but it's the only sheet metal shop in town. My little 3D printing sideline is the only thing that grows if I push it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Kessler and try to get on the laser cutter, which pays a bit more. I'd put more evenings into the printing shop, aiming for an extra hundred a month. And I'd keep using AI for the designs, because it saves me hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mildly frustrated. I like big change, and this is the opposite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is the printing shop doing now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sell clips for camper van curtains and replacement knobs for old cookers, about forty quid a month. It covers the printer filament and my phone bill. The 3D-printed cooker knobs I sell online are weirdly popular with old ladies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Kessler has a bad year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the forty becomes important fast. Lena and I have about three weeks of rent saved between us. I'd try to grow the sideline to cover the gas bill, at least.

say: I'd say the plateau is a **let-down**, but the AI tools are still handy at work.
I'd post that AI is **still useful**, just not magic.
think: Nothing changes for the job, and the **pay stays low** at Kessler.
My **3D printing** sideline is the only thing that grows if I push.
do: Ask to move onto the **laser cutter**, which pays a bit more.
Grow the printing shop to an **extra hundred** a month.
Keep using AI to speed up **part designs** in the evenings.
feel: He feels **mildly frustrated**, because he likes big change.
S0.quote: The 3D-printed cooker knobs I sell online are weirdly popular with old ladies.
fieldNote: His job is steady but **low pay** and three weeks of savings keep him uneasy.
The **sideline** is his own lever, and he wants it to grow.
He uses AI **daily** at work and at home without fuss.

steps.text: Ask to be trained on Kessler's laser cutter
Grow the 3D-printed parts shop to an extra hundred a month
Use AI design tools to speed up new part designs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly good news if you're willing to learn. At work I'd show people how to use the new software instead of fearing it. Online I'd keep it practical, how-to posts, not opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the office at Kessler shrinks: the person who draws the parts and the person who orders steel get software. The press brakes still need people for a while, and the new bending robots are pricey. I'd want to be the guy who can do both, fold and program.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to learn the offline programming software, where you set up the bends on a computer before they reach the machine. I'd do an online course in CAD, which is computer drawing, maybe thirty a month. And I'd keep the sideline going as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly upbeat, with a bit of guilt about the office folk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would you feel guilty about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Graham, who draws the counters, is in his fifties. Our draughtsman Graham still uses a mouse like it's a bar of soap. If AI does his drawings, part of his job comes to me, and I don't love that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say that to Graham's face?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to show him the tools, quietly, at lunch. He might tell me where to go, which is fair. But I'd rather offer than not.

say: I'd say Steady Disruption is **good news** if you're willing to learn.
I'd post **how-to** guides rather than opinions online.
think: Kessler's office shrinks as **drawing and ordering** go to software.
I want to be the one who can **fold and program** the machines.
do: Learn the **offline programming** software for setting up bends on screen.
Pay about thirty a month for an **online CAD** course.
Keep the **printing sideline** going as a backup.
feel: He feels **fairly upbeat** about his chances.
He feels **guilty** about the office staff.
S1.quote: Our draughtsman Graham still uses a mouse like it's a bar of soap.
fieldNote: He sees the office shrinking as **his opening**.
His guilt about **Graham** shows he notices who pays the price.
His own job looks safe for now, so **uneasy** fits better than anxious.

steps.text: Learn Kessler's offline bend programming software
Take a thirty-a-month online CAD course
Keep selling 3D-printed parts as a backup income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and we need proper rules fast, like some income support for people who get pushed out. At work I'd say learn everything you can in the next two years. Online I'd share the useful stuff, not the doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me more than I'd admit. By 2028 the drawing and programming I was learning go to AI, and by 2031 the robot folds better than me. I'd be 31 with skills that expired twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd skip the CAD course and learn robot maintenance instead, because hands-on lasts the extra three years. I'd push the sideline hard, maybe repairing 3D printers for other people. And Lena and I would move in with her parents for a year to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm the guy who loves new tech, and even I can't see where I land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does moving in with Lena's parents mean for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her dad and I get on fine, but the house is small and her brother still lives there. We'd lose privacy, and Lena would hate it more than me. We'd do it for a year, maybe eighteen months, to save a real cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to friends who think you'll be fine because you're good with tech?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them being good with apps doesn't mean anything when the apps can do the job themselves. Being early with new tech helps you for a year, not forever. That's the honest version.

say: I'd say we need **proper rules** fast, including income support.
I'd tell coworkers to **learn everything** they can in two years.
think: The **drawing and programming** I was learning go to AI by 2028.
By 2031 the robot folds better, so my skills **expire twice**.
do: Switch from CAD to **robot maintenance** training this year.
Repair **3D printers** for other people to boost the sideline.
Move in with **Lena's parents** for a year to save.
feel: He feels **alarmed**, despite loving new tech.
S2.quote: Being early with new tech helps you for a year, not forever.
fieldNote: Even this **early adopter** loses confidence with two years' warning.
He catches that the **thinking skills** he was learning go before his hands-on job.
Moving in with **Lena's parents** is a real sacrifice for both.

steps.text: Drop the CAD course and train in robot maintenance
Offer a 3D printer repair service alongside selling parts
Move in with Lena's parents for a year to save

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent runway if people use it. At work I'd organise a little lunchtime session showing people AI tools. Online I'd stay practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to earn a bit from the in-between stuff. Learning bend programming now pays off until about 2031. After that, I'd want to be in robot maintenance before 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd do the bend programming and ask for a pay rise once I can do it. Then I'd start an evening course in mechatronics, the mix of mechanics and electronics. I'd grow the sideline into a little repair service and save the profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but energised. Like a long climb where I can see the top, even if it's a false summit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a false summit mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's when you climb a hill and find another hill behind it. Robot maintenance might be a false summit, because the robots get better at fixing themselves after 2034. I'd still climb, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep your savings up while studying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every pound from the sideline goes in a separate account, not touched. Lena would keep her salon money for the bills. Hopefully a couple of thousand by year three.

say: I'd say five years is a **decent runway** if people use it.
I'd run a **lunchtime session** showing coworkers AI tools.
think: Bend programming pays off **until about 2031**, then it fades.
I'd want to move into **robot maintenance** before 2034.
do: Learn **bend programming** and ask for a pay rise once I can do it.
Start an evening **mechatronics** course after the first year.
Put all **sideline profits** into a separate account.
feel: He feels **anxious but energised**, like a long climb.
S3.quote: Robot maintenance might be a false summit, because the robots get better at fixing themselves after 2034.
fieldNote: He times his skills to the **gap** between AGI and robots.
Admits the end goal might be a **false summit**.
His job still goes eventually, so mood is **anxious**, not uneasy.

steps.text: Learn bend programming and then ask Kessler for a raise
Start an evening mechatronics course in the second year
Bank every pound of sideline profit in a separate account
Run lunchtime sessions showing coworkers the AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people to get ready, if they start now. At work I'd talk up courses. Online I'd share small wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years lets me build something of my own, not just a CV. By 2036 I could have a small repair business with a van. I'd be 40 when robots match people, and I'd want to own the robots, not compete with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at Kessler while doing evening mechatronics. In a few years I'd buy a second-hand van and start a repair business for printers and small machines. I'd save every month and maybe put a bit into a cheap index fund, which is a basket of shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic, with a little voice saying the end point is still the end point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes owning the robots better than competing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a robot can fix printers, I'd rather be the one sending it out and taking the money. My grandad had his own garage, and he always said own the tools, don't be the tool. That stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could stop that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money mostly. A van, tools and a few robots cost more than I'll ever save on this pay. I'd need a loan or a partner, and Lena would need convincing.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** if people start now.
I'd talk up **courses** at work and share small wins.
think: Ten years lets me build a **business of my own**.
I'd want to **own the robots**, not compete with them by 2039.
do: Study **evening mechatronics** while keeping the Kessler job.
Buy a **second-hand van** for a repair business in a few years.
Put a little into a **cheap index fund** each month.
feel: He feels **optimistic**, with a doubt about the end point.
S4.quote: My grandad had his own garage, and he always said own the tools, don't be the tool.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his worry into a **business plan**.
He knows **money** is the main barrier on his pay.
Still expects his press job to go, so **anxious** fits despite the optimism.

steps.text: Study evening mechatronics while staying at Kessler
Buy a second-hand van and start a small machine repair business

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because the skills I'd be learning would expire before I finished. What would help is cheap loans for small businesses and training that isn't out of date before you start. And maybe a basic income floor while people switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the 3D printing. People like me with small sidelines could be the start of something, if we had a bit of backing. My cooker knobs won't save the economy, but they're mine.

headlineQuote: My cooker knobs won't save the economy, but they're mine.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old** press brake operator at Kessler Metalcraft, still learning his angles.
He uses AI tools **daily**, at work and for a small 3D printing sideline.
He lives with Lena, a **trainee hairdresser**, on low pay and three weeks of savings.
He sees Steady Disruption as his **opening**, but AGI by 2028 frightens even him.
With ten years he aims to **own a repair business** rather than compete with robots.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his **new skills** would expire before he finished.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **cheap business loans** and training that stays current.
He wants a **basic income floor** while people switch.
